title: Lesson 2: Four pathways to impact
html:
Most people think about doing good through a single lens — usually donations or volunteering. But you have at least four distinct resources you can direct toward your chosen problem: your career, your money, your political voice, and your ability to help others have more impact. These pathways interact and compound. A career in policy gives you a platform for advocacy. Giving connects you to a community of effective donors. Helping others find impactful careers multiplies your efforts many times over.

But the four pathways are not equally important, and not equally easy — and it’s worth saying so plainly, because it’s the reason this week is shaped the way it is.

Your career is the most important. The case for this claim rests on two facts. First, scale: a typical career is around 80,000 hours of work — your single biggest resource for helping others, far larger than anything you’ll do on the side, so increasing the impact of those hours even slightly outweighs almost any other change you could make. Second, variation: some career paths let you do vastly more good than others — plausibly 10, 100, even 1,000 times more — and that spread is far wider than people expect. Put the two together and the conclusion is hard to escape: thinking carefully about how you use your career is one of the most powerful choices you can make. That’s why it gets the most time this week.

Your giving is the easiest. You can act on it today, at any level, and scale up as you go — no retraining, no job change, low commitment, and reversible. That makes it the most reliable way to do a lot of good right now, especially while the slower work on your career is still playing out. We keep this part short and practical: the brevity reflects how easy it is to start, not how little good it can do.

Your political voice can be powerful. Policy shapes outcomes for millions, and a vote, a letter to a representative, a donation to a campaign or a well-placed conversation can all nudge it. How much this fits you depends on your platform and your appetite for it, so treat it as worth doing where you have an opening rather than a box everyone must tick.

Being a multiplier compounds other people’s efforts. If you help one person shift towards high-impact work, or help ten think harder about where they give, you multiply your own impact through other people — which is why it’s among the most underrated pathways. Like political voice, how much it applies depends on your situation, so add it where it fits.

The goal isn’t to max out all four at once — that’s the road to burnout. It’s to take the career question seriously, start giving now, and add political voice and multiplier work where they suit you.

Case study: how many lives does a doctor save?

Here’s a claim to sit with: over an entire career, the average doctor in a rich country saves only a handful of lives. Not one a week, the way the medical dramas suggest — a few, in total, across forty years of work. That’s roughly where 80,000 Hours lands, and following how they get there is about the clearest demonstration there is of why your gut feeling about a career’s impact can’t be trusted.

Start with the big picture. UK life expectancy roughly doubled over two centuries, from about 40 to about 80. It’s tempting to credit modern medicine — antibiotics, surgery, vaccines. But most of that gain came from the social determinants of health: rising wealth, better nutrition, sanitation, public-health knowledge and safer work. The clearest tell is timing. Tuberculosis mortality had already fallen by about 30% before the bacterium was even identified, about 80% before there was an effective drug, and about 90% before a vaccine. Health spending exploded after life expectancy rose, not before; and when researchers randomised people to more or less healthcare access (the Oregon and RAND experiments), the health gains were minor.

Medicine still matters — just less than the tropes suggest. Insulin turned type-1 diabetes from a death sentence into a manageable condition, and vaccines did dramatic work against polio and smallpox. But as a share of the whole, medical care is a minor player. One careful estimate credits it with about 5 of those ~30 added years of life, plus roughly another 5 years of relief from poorer health. Turn that into a rough number — spread across the population and divided among the UK’s ~3 doctors per 1,000 people — and a doctor’s entire career comes to very roughly 70 “lives saved,” or a couple of lives a year. Respectable, and better than most jobs, but a long way from the medical-drama image of saving someone every shift.

Now the part that really matters for your career. Even that figure is an overestimate, because it credits one doctor with health that many people and forces produced together. The right question isn’t “how much good does medicine do?” but “how much more good happens because I become a doctor?” In a country that already trains plenty of doctors, if you don’t take the place at medical school, someone else does — and the competition for those places is fierce. Once you account for that replaceability, and for diminishing returns in a country that already has many doctors, 80,000 Hours estimates the marginal impact of one extra UK doctor is closer to a few lives over a whole career — not a couple a year.

Notice what just happened. The intuitive answer — “medicine is about as impactful a career as there is” — survived contact with neither the evidence on what actually drives health nor the questions of counterfactual and marginal impact. That’s the whole point of thinking carefully: your first guess about where you’ll do the most good is often wrong, sometimes by a lot. It’s also why the same person might do far more good as a doctor where doctors are actually scarce, by earning to give, or by working on a neglected problem like pandemic preparedness — options the headline figure hides completely. (80,000 Hours, “How many lives does a doctor save?”)

Your career

Your career is roughly 80,000 hours — your biggest opportunity for impact. Here is 80,000 Hours’ entire career guide, distilled to a sentence: do what matters — build useful skills, and use them to help others.
